items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: One of them was Jimmie Rowles’s daughter, Stacey Rowles.

ctx.x: You were – can you go into a little bit more about the all-girl band?

Yeah. I was with – I was about to say, the purpose of my saying – I was with the festival, and I suggested to them something that – first of all, I saved it by having a group of my friends come out, name people, and doing the festival for very little money to get it back on track. That worked, so then the next year I told them, said, “Let’s try an all-girls band.” They said, “Oh yeah? Sure.” We had good charts. I had the people there to agree to take in two or three girls for 10 days while we rehearsed and…

had a little lead trumpet player. She was very stocky built, and a short neck. She could shake on a high G [Terry imitates the sound]. We had a drummer from a university in Michigan. Some – I don’t know what the name of the university was, but she had long red hair, and she played with her hair hanging down over her face. It looked like just a glob of red hair playing. She would shake her hair and play, but you never could see – part the hair to see her face. She was a marvelous little drummer. Then the bass…

items.title: 68145_Jimmie Rowles oral history interview
items.q: The interviewer mentions Clark Terry in the context of an album 'Tell It Like It Is' and compares his style to the interviewee's, but the interviewee does not explicitly confirm a personal relationship, only commenting on the interviewer's statement about Clark being a 'dapper, natty dresser'.

ctx.x: met Clark Terry... She knows all of them...you know, Freddie Hubbard... I don't know if she knows Wynton Marsalis or not. She knows Dizzy very well, you know... And they all respect her very highly. And we just made this album called Tell It Like It Is, and everybody seems to like it.
